🔻 Iran emerged more united, stronger from recent war: Senior lawmaker

📌 Mashhad, IRNA – Deputy Parliament Speaker Ali Nikzad says the recent war failed to weaken or divide Iran; instead, it strengthened national unity and preserved the country’s defense and strategic capabilities.

Speaking at a meeting of senior managers of the State Welfare Organization of Iran in Mashhad on Tuesday, Razavi Khorasan Province, the legislator said the United States had entered the conflict believing it could end the war quickly and at low cost, even within 72 hours.
​
He said adversaries sought to destroy Iran’s nuclear capabilities, naval forces and other strategic assets while creating conditions for political change and control over the country’s oil resources.
​
Nikzad said attempts to create social divisions through infiltration also failed, arguing that public solidarity strengthened the country’s resistance. He said Iran was not fragmented but became more united, while its oil exports, naval forces and air capabilities remained intact and, in some areas, grew stronger.
​
He also highlighted the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz and added that adversaries had failed to remove Iran’s enriched uranium from the country.
​
Nikzad said that the Islamic Republic had warned regional neighbors against allowing their territory to be used for attacks on Iran.
​
He praised Imam Khomeini’s leadership legacy, citing faith, courage, reliance on God, decisiveness, and belief in national capabilities. He also honored the country’s martyred Leader Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khemenei for his political wisdom and steadfast commitment to disadvantaged groups and national interests.

🛢 Oil executives: Global fuel crisis already underway amid prolonged Hormuz blockade — Bloomberg

Heads of major oil companies say a large-scale fuel crisis has already begun as the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz drags on.

Trump administration officials insist the disruptions to the oil market are temporary, but experts at Chevron and other companies warn that strategic reserves are nearly depleted, with no signs of improvement in sight.

A recent strike on a pipeline in Saudi Arabia has made things worse, knocking at least 2.5 million barrels per day off the global oil market.

Experts warn that without a visible resolution to the conflict with Iran, the situation risks spiraling out of control.

China is partly fueling the global supply deficit. The world's largest oil importer covered nearly half its daily consumption from its own crude reserves for months, giving oil markets some breathing room — but analysts say in recent weeks Beijing has resumed larger purchases from international suppliers.
